gaps.title: Persistent specialist threads resume only for human @mentions — every operator-initiated run is a fresh session with no canonical anchor
gaps.what_is_absent: There is no path by which the operator re-runs an already-engaged agent on its existing provider session, and no path by which a fresh specialist run receives the canonical task state. `startAgentRun` (app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts:650) always mints a new thread id (:1033-1035) and calls `startRun` (:1071) with no `resumeSessionId`. Session resume exists — `resumeRun` (app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts:659) — but its only production caller is app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:1237, the human-@mention/comment reply path. Separately, `canonicalTaskAnchor` (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:956) is invoked only at :1182 and :1189, inside that same reply path; the fresh-run prompt builders `buildAnalyzePrompt` (specialist-run.server.ts:1409) and `buildSpecialistPersona` (:1205) contain role, title, goal, repo/branch contract, directive, trust boundary — and no timeline, no prior verdict, no decision history, no anchor block. The workspace clone is reused, so code context survives; conversational and decision context does not.
gaps.why_it_matters: The rework loop is the core daily motion: reviewer requests changes, operator re-prompts the deliverer, reviewer re-reviews. Today each of those turns is a stateless agent that knows only what the operator retyped into its directive. A reviewer re-run on revision 2 has no memory of what it asked for on revision 1 and cannot tell whether its own request was honoured; the deliverer has no memory of why it made the choices sitting in its own branch. Continuity is entirely mediated by operator prose, which is exactly the "context rebuilt from scattered notes" problem the product exists to remove.
gaps.intent_basis: FR22 ("Persistent agent threads can be resumed across stages and later consultations"); MVP Phase-1 bullet "One delivering engagement plus persistent supporting engagements"; the Differentiators section ("persistent specialists that can be re-engaged over time, materially different from stateless automations or isolated agent chats"); Domain requirement Runtime continuity ("Any reactivated agent re-anchors on the canonical task artifact before acting"). Not on the INTENT.md §6 deliberate-divergence list.
gaps.evidence_of_absence: grep for `resumeSessionId` across app/ returns only the two runtime adapters, adapter.server.ts, run-service.server.ts and run-sink.server.ts — no caller in specialist-run.server.ts. grep for `resumeRun(` returns exactly two hits: the definition and task-actions.server.ts:1237. planning/discovery-2026-08-06-pass19/reference/AGENTS-RUNTIME.md §1 states independently: "Its one production caller is `task-actions.server.ts:1217` (dynamic import)". `canonicalTaskAnchor` has three call sites, all in the reply path. The fresh-run prompt text was read end to end (specialist-run.server.ts:1409-1565): it contains no history.
gaps.owner_question: Should an operator-initiated run of an already-engaged agent resume that agent's session (as the @mention path does), or is the intended model "one fresh session per turn, re-anchored on task.md" — in which case the fresh-run prompt needs the canonical anchor block that today only the resume path gets?
gaps.partial:
PARTIAL — the plumbing exists and is high quality; the missing piece is who can pull it and what a cold start receives.

EXISTS (do not list these as absent):
1. `resumeRun` (app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts:659) is a complete, production-wired resume: it re-applies the full run confinement (disallowedTools, native skills, allowedTools, env/GIT_CEILING, MCP servers, systemPrompt/persona, Codex outputSchema), carries agent identity for Agent-logs grouping, applies the profile's CURRENT model/effort, and pre-probes provider transcript continuity — on `missing` it records `session_missing`, writes a continuity note, and cold-starts with a `continuityResetPreamble` instead of handing a dead id to the SDK (:722-760). The UI renders resume boundaries (`RUN_BOUNDARY_TAG` / "── resumed · run N of M ──", app/features/runtime/runtime-types.ts:79-96) and offers session export so a human can continue the same session on their own machine (app/features/runtime/runs-panels.tsx:285-325).
2. `canonicalTaskAnchor` (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:956) is a real canonical-state block — goal, stage, readiness, waiting, validation, delivery refs (branch/PR), any open decision packet WITH its options, and the newest N timeline events, prompt-budget clamped. Covered by a dedicated suite, app/server/tasks/canonical-anchor.server.test.ts (including "a RESUMED specialist re-anchors on the EDITED goal (UC-30)").
3. The claim's "resume only for human @mentions" is imprecise. There are TWO product triggers that resume, and the second is a numbered ruling: R15-14 / decisions.md ruling 33 — a resolved `ask_human` decision packet goes back to the AGENT THAT ASKED by resuming its own session. `answerAskingAgent` (task-actions.server.ts:636, called at :4824) addresses the agent by the same @handle a human would type and routes through `commentToAgent`, so it inherits resume + confinement + anchor; the operator hand-off is only the fallback when the session or profile is gone. The toolkit promises this to the model verbatim (agent-toolkit.server.ts:250, specialist-run.server.ts:992: "You WILL be resumed in this same session with the decision"). So the governance loop (agent asks → human decides → agent continues) already closes on the same thread. It is still a single code path (`commentToAgent`), which is why the greps returned one caller.

GENUINELY ABSENT:
a. No operator-initiated resume. Neither `run_agent` nor `prompt_agent` can continue an already-engaged agent's session — both always cold-start. In the common loop (operator prompts deliverer → reviewer requests changes → operator re-prompts deliverer for rework), the deliverer is a brand-new session every time, with only the operator's directive prose as continuity.
b. No canonical anchor on any fresh run. `buildAnalyzePrompt` gives role, title, goal, workspace/delivery contract, the pinned `reviewSubject` head SHA for reviewers, the directive (+`directiveFrom`), and the trust boundary — and no timeline, no prior verdict, no open packet, no decision history. Note this also bites the @mention path on a FIRST mention: with no prior session, `commentToAgent` falls to `startAgentRun` (:1259-1330) and the anchor is dropped; the anchor rides `specialistReplyDirective` only.
c. No pull-side substitute for (b). The specialist MCP server `viberr_agent` exposes exactly three tools — post_comment, ask_human, report_outcome (agent-toolkit.server.ts:222/249/304) — with no task-read tool, and the run cwd is "ALWAYS an isolated workspace dir … NEVER the task dir" (specialist-run.server.ts:866-873), so task.md is unreadable from the workspace. The workspace clone preserves code context; conversational/decision context has no channel.
d. No human-facing control to resume a specific run/session other than @mentioning the agent (runs-panels offers export-for-local-CLI, not in-app resume).

The cheapest closure follows the shape already ruled correct in R15-14: pass `canonicalTaskAnchor` into `buildAnalyzePrompt` for every fresh run (closes b and c, and makes cold starts honest against FR22's "even with no runtime history"), and give `operatorRunAgent`/`operatorPromptAgent` the same resume-if-a-session-exists branch `commentToAgent` already has (closes a). Neither is on the INTENT.md §6 deliberate-divergence list.

gaps.title: Dismissing an operator recommendation leaves no trace on the canonical record, and the operator cannot see its own pending recommendations
gaps.what_is_absent: `dismissRecommendation` (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:5938-5987) removes the recommendation from frontmatter and writes an audit row (`task.recommendation.dismissed`, :5977) — and nothing else. No timeline event, no note, no packet. The task file, which is the thing every future agent re-anchors on, never records that a human declined. Compounding it: `OperatorTaskSnapshot` (app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts:1364-1410) has no `recommendations` field at all, so the operator's `get_task` cannot see pending or resolved recommendation cards; its only window is `recentTimeline` (:1527, `slice(0, 6)`). And `addRecommendation`'s duplicate guard (:561-566) compares only against currently-pending recommendations, so once a card is dismissed the identical card can be re-added.
gaps.why_it_matters: This is Journey 2's loop and it can spin. A supervisor declines "move to Review"; the operator's next turn sees no dismissal, has no list of what it already proposed, and re-proposes it. The human declines again. Nothing in the durable record ever explains why the move was refused, so the refusal is unavailable to the next agent, to a later reviewer, or to anyone reading the task after the 90-day audit window closes. "Dismiss" is one of the two answers a supervisor gives a recommendation, and it is the one that writes nothing down.
gaps.intent_basis: FR33 ("preserve an auditable history of human decisions") is met only in the 90-day audit table, not in the canonical record FR12 defines as authoritative; PRD Success Criteria ("a user can quickly see … the latest decision or blocker"); MVP bullet "Typed important events for … transition requests, blocked decisions"; Journey 2 (the operator "updates the flow" after a human decision).
gaps.evidence_of_absence: Read `dismissRecommendation` in full — the single `updateTaskFile` callback (:5967-5971) only filters the recommendations array; there is no `parsed.timeline.unshift` anywhere in the function. Contrast `resolvePacket` (:4376+), which writes a typed `**Decision:** …` event for every one of the nine option kinds, and `applyRecommendation` (:5757+), whose inner governed mutations each write their own typed event. grep for `recommendations` in operator-actions.server.ts returns only :561 and :568, both inside `addRecommendation`.
gaps.owner_question: Should a dismissal write a typed timeline event naming what was declined (and optionally a reason), and should the operator snapshot carry its own pending/recently-resolved recommendations so it can stop re-proposing a declined move?
gaps.partial: The claim is correct, and one part is understated. WHAT EXISTS: (1) the recommendation's CREATION is on the canonical record — addRecommendation (operator-actions.server.ts:556-575) unshifts a `**Recommendation:** {label}. {reasoning}` operator comment into the timeline, notifies mentioned users, and pings supervisors via notifyTaskWatchers, so the ASK is durably recorded and can appear in the operator's recentTimeline; (2) applyRecommendation leaves a trace indirectly — its inner governed mutation (transition/assign/accept) writes its own typed event, mirroring resolvePacket's `**Decision:** …` events (task-actions.server.ts:4607-4724); (3) dismissal does write an audit row (`task.recommendation.dismissed`, :5977) with kind+label details, and the UI shows a transient toast (`Dismissed · {label}`, app/routes/project.task.tsx:695); (4) the server-side runtime is not blind to pending recommendations — operatorLeftTaskStranded (app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts:419-431) reads frontmatter.recommendations to decide whether to resume a stranded drive. WHAT IS NOT THERE: (a) no timeline event, note, comment or packet on dismissal, so task.md — the artifact every future agent and every human re-anchors on — records "operator recommended X" and then X silently vanishes with no answer; (b) WORSE THAN CLAIMED, the audit row has no reader at all: the activity page's audit panel filters on an explicit whitelist, AUDIT_ACTION_KINDS in app/server/projections/activity-feed.server.ts:113-148, which contains neither task.recommendation.dismissed nor .applied (listAuditLog and countAuditLog both use `action IN (…)` over exactly those keys), and POLICY_AUDIT_ACTIONS (app/features/policy/policy-query.server.ts:42-49) omits it too — so the row is invisible in the product and is hard-deleted at 90 days by app/server/db/retention.server.ts:72. INTENT.md:151 justifies that 90-day bound on the premise that "Task-scoped history survives in task.md", which is exactly the premise this path breaks; (c) the operator's get_task cannot see pending or resolved recommendation cards — no recommendations field in the snapshot, so a re-invoked operator cannot tell that a human declined its proposal; (d) no dismissal memory: the dup guard compares only against currently-pending cards and grep for "dismissed" finds no frontmatter field, column, or store, so the identical card is re-added on the next drive and, because wasNew flips true again, re-notifies the same supervisors. Net effect a real team hits: a human declines an operator proposal, the operator re-runs, proposes the identical thing, re-pings the bell, and nothing on the task or in any UI records that the human already said no.

gaps.title: The five anti-noise guardrails have no configuration surface anywhere in the app
gaps.what_is_absent: No route, loader or panel reads or writes the five anti-noise guardrails. They are seeded ON at project creation (app/features/home/project-create.server.ts:294-296 from DEFAULT_GUARDRAILS, app/shared/workflow/templates.ts:81-87) and read at enforcement time (`guardrailOn`/`guardrailValue`, app/server/tasks/comment-guardrails.server.ts:182-212) — but nothing in between. The only guardrail row an admin can change in-app is `delete-branch-after-merge` (app/features/project-settings/settings-actions.server.ts:168-193), which is not one of the five. The `compression-threshold` value (seeded 40) and the 1000-char operator-brevity cap are likewise unreachable. Because `guardrailOn` returns false for an absent row (:191-195), a project created directly in the file-native store — which FR10 explicitly supports — has all five silently off, with no surface that would reveal it.
gaps.why_it_matters: The PRD names timeline noise the product's #1 adoption risk and lists these five as an MVP feature. They work — but a team that finds operator narration trimmed too aggressively, or wants compaction to start at 100 events instead of 40, has no in-product answer; the only remedy is hand-editing project.md YAML. Journey 3 (Elif front-loads project design) has no place to make this decision, and no admin can even confirm the guardrails are on.
gaps.intent_basis: MVP Phase-1 bullet "Anti-noise guardrails: meaningful-comment, operator brevity, no-duplicate-summary, compression-threshold, evidence-separation"; FR6/FR8 (admins define project policy); Journey 3. The `value`/`unit` fields in `guardrailSchema` (app/schemas/project-file.schema.ts:155-163) model a tunable that nothing exposes.
gaps.evidence_of_absence: grep -rl "guardrail" over app/features and app/routes returns exactly: project-create.server.ts, settings-actions.server.ts, resources-panel.tsx and agents-page.tsx (the last two use the word only in unrelated code comments). Neither app/features/project-settings/settings-query.server.ts nor app/features/policy/policy-query.server.ts mentions `guardrails`. Section headings: policy page = Human access · RBAC / Agent capability / Workflow rules; project settings = Project / Workflow stages / Members / Repository & credentials / Danger zone. Note that comment-guardrails.server.ts:5-10 still describes them as "rendered in settings", which is no longer true of the shipped tree.
gaps.owner_question: Do the five anti-noise guardrails belong on the Policy page as a project-policy block (toggles plus the compression threshold), or are they deliberately fixed product behavior — in which case should the per-project rows and the `value` field be collapsed to constants so the file stops implying configurability?
gaps.partial:
The claim is accurate; it partially exists in one narrow sense worth stating precisely.

WHAT EXISTS
1. Enforcement is real and complete for all five: `meaningful-comment` (task-actions.server.ts:1473, operator-actions.server.ts:407/413), `evidence-separation` (:1478, :408), `operator-brevity` (:409, hard cap in comment-guardrails.server.ts:51), `no-duplicate-summary` (operator-actions.server.ts:433), `compression-threshold` incl. the tunable `value` (task-actions.server.ts:813-814, :1563-1564; operator-actions.server.ts:434-435).
2. Per-event DISCLOSURE exists — the only place a user ever learns a guardrail acted. Inline trim markers in the record ("_(trimmed by the operator-brevity guardrail …)_", comment-guardrails.server.ts:51; the evidence-separation marker at :77) and an honest NOOP message back to the agent ("NOT posted — the meaningful-comment guardrail dropped it as status chatter", :161; the no-duplicate-summary equivalent at :164), plus an audit row. So the guardrails announce themselves when they fire.
3. The persistence layer is complete: `guardrailSchema` models `on`/`value`/`unit` (project-file.schema.ts:155-163), the frontmatter field is required (:190), and it is projected to `projects.guardrails_json` (rebuilder.server.ts:190-214) and mapped to a typed `Guardrail[]` (app/shared/mapping/project.server.ts:45/67).
4. Exactly one guardrail row is writable in-app: `delete-branch-after-merge`, via `setBranchCleanup` (settings-actions.server.ts:168-193, R15-6, `edit-policy` tier), surfaced as a toggle on the settings page (settings-page.tsx:1114) and covered by tests (settings-page.test.tsx:652-681). It reuses the guardrail row as storage but is not one of the PRD five.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST
No loader exposes the five to any page, no action writes them, no panel renders them — not even read-only. An admin cannot see whether they are on, cannot turn one off, and cannot retune `compression-threshold` (seeded 40 events) or the operator-brevity character cap (hard-coded in comment-guardrails.server.ts, not even modelled as a `value`). The `value`/`unit` schema fields are written once by the seed and read only by enforcement.

TWO NOTES THAT SHARPEN THE GAP
- `guardrailOn` returns `false` for an absent row (comment-guardrails.server.ts:190-194) and the parser's `tolerant()` fallback for a malformed `guardrails` block is `[]` (project-file.schema.ts:454-459). So a project authored directly in the file-native store, or one whose guardrail block fails to parse, runs with all five silently OFF and there is no surface anywhere — settings, policy, or a diagnostics panel — that would reveal it. The only diagnostics panel in the UI (task-detail/task-main-sections.tsx:42) renders task diagnostics, not project-file parse diagnostics.
- The module doc at comment-guardrails.server.ts:5-7 still says these were "rendered in settings with zero enforcement code" — describing the pre-Q3 state. Enforcement was added and the rendering was never (re)built, so the comment is now inverted relative to the shipped tree.

gaps.title: Two of the five guardrails cover only operator narration comments — decision packets, the surface the brevity guardrail's own copy names, are exempt
gaps.what_is_absent: `no-duplicate-summary` and `operator-brevity` are enforced at exactly one call site: `applyCommentGuardrails` from app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts:405, the operator's narration comment path (dedupe at :433-444 against the last operator comment only). Nothing applies them to decision packets: `operatorOpenPacket` builds `body` and `observations` with a bare `.trim()` (operator-actions.server.ts:783-797) and posts them with no guardrail pass — yet the shipped description of operator-brevity is "Operator packets keep to observed → changed → recommended → decision required" (app/shared/workflow/templates.ts:83). Agent reports are also outside the dedupe: the agent-reply path (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:1466-1480) applies only `meaningful-comment` and `evidence-separation`, so a re-run reviewer that emits a byte-identical report posts it twice, while no-duplicate-summary's description is authored unscoped ("A summary that restates an earlier one is dropped instead of appended", templates.ts:85).
gaps.why_it_matters: Packets are the highest-stakes prose in the product — the thing Journey 2 says must be "concise" for a blocked task to reach a human decision quickly — and they are the one operator surface with no length discipline. Duplicate agent reports are the concrete daily flood (re-run a reviewer twice on an unchanged revision), and that is exactly the case the dedupe guardrail's copy promises to catch.
gaps.intent_basis: MVP bullet listing all five guardrails; the shipped guardrail descriptions in app/shared/workflow/templates.ts:83 and :85; PRD Measurable outcomes ("low friction from duplicated summaries or raw validation spam"); Journey 2 ("The packet is concise").
gaps.evidence_of_absence: grep for `enforceOperatorBrevity|separateEvidence` in operator-actions.server.ts returns nothing outside the `applyCommentGuardrails` import; grep for `no-duplicate-summary` across app/ returns four hits, all in the operator narration path or the copy strings. `prepareAgentReplyEvent` was read in full (task-actions.server.ts:1457-1496): two guardrails, no dedupe, no brevity. The packet builder was read in full: no guardrail call.
gaps.owner_question: Should operator-brevity and evidence-separation run over packet bodies and observations (matching the copy that already claims they do), and should no-duplicate-summary extend to agent reports — or should both descriptions be narrowed to say "operator comments" and the packet stay uncapped by design?
gaps.partial:
PARTIALLY EXISTS — precisely what is and is not there.

WHAT EXISTS (all real, none decorative):
- comment-guardrails.server.ts implements `isMeaninglessComment` (:28), `enforceOperatorBrevity` (:38, cap `OPERATOR_BREVITY_MAX_CHARS = 1000`), `separateEvidence` (:63, `EVIDENCE_MAX_FENCE_LINES = 12`), and `applyCommentGuardrails` (:113) which reports what it did via `CommentTrim`/`CommentDropReason` plus `commentOutcomeMessage` (:157) so the model is told "NOT posted" rather than "posted".
- `applyCommentGuardrails` DOES support dedupe generically: it takes `noDuplicate` + `previousText` (:115-120, check at :145-150). The capability is built; it is simply never passed by the two non-operator callers.
- Operator narration path (writeOperatorComment, operator-actions.server.ts:385-471) is the only place all five fire: meaningful/evidence/brevity via the shared helper (:405-410), timeline-based dedupe (:433-445), compression-threshold (:434-465), with `recordCommentDrop` audit rows on both drop reasons.
- Agent reply path (prepareAgentReplyEvent, task-actions.server.ts:1457-1496) fires meaningful-comment + evidence-separation only; compression-threshold was later added for agent-reply floods at :1560-1563 (comment cites G7/B-FD9).

WHAT IS NOT THERE:
1. No guardrail of any kind touches a decision packet — not operator packets, not agent question packets, not stuck-loop packets. `packet.body` and `packet.observations[].v` reach task.md untrimmed and unbounded, so a 20k-char body or a 400-line pasted log inside an observation lands verbatim in the canonical record that every future agent prompt re-anchors on. That is the exact failure evidence-separation and brevity were built to prevent, on the surface the PRD's Journey 2 calls "concise".
2. No dedupe on agent reports. A re-run reviewer emitting a byte-identical report posts it twice; nothing compares against the prior comment.
3. The operator dedupe is narrower than its copy claims: it compares only against the single most recent operator comment (`parsed.timeline.find(...)` at :438-441), so an A/B/A restatement is not caught, while templates.ts:85 is authored unscoped ("A summary that restates an earlier one is dropped instead of appended").

ONE IMPORTANT NUANCE THE CLAIM UNDERSTATES — the packet is not unguarded prose end to end. Its SHAPE is enforced structurally by the type rather than by a text guardrail: `operatorOpenPacket` validates every option kind against `PACKET_KIND_SET` (:718-726), forces exactly one `rec` option (:757-778), refuses a second packet while one is open (:735-746, re-checked inside the locked write at :801), and the packet carries typed `observations[{k,v,code}]`. So "observed → changed → recommended → decision required" is delivered for packets as a data model. What is absent is the noise control — the char cap and the evidence trim — plus dedupe.

Also worth flagging for the copy, though it is a defect not a gap: the "observed → changed → recommended → decision required" phrasing that templates.ts:84 attributes to *packets* is actually the prompt instruction on the operator's COMMENT tool (operator-toolkit.server.ts:184 and operator-run.server.ts:916). The guardrail's description names the one surface it does not touch, while the surface it does touch is described nowhere.

Smallest honest fix: route packet `body` and each non-`code` observation value through `applyCommentGuardrails({evidence, brevity})` in `operatorOpenPacket` and `openAgentQuestionPacket`, and pass `noDuplicate` + the prior comment by the same actor in `prepareAgentReplyEvent`.

gaps.title: Transition requests and non-blocking decision requests are written as plain comments, so the request itself is compaction-eligible
gaps.what_is_absent: No typed event marks a transition being *requested*. `addRecommendation` writes the "**Recommendation:** …" narration as `type: "comment"` (app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts:571-580), and an `input`-type decision packet writes "**Decision packet:** …" as `type: "comment"` too — only `blocked` packets get a typed event (operator-actions.server.ts:816-828). Both then satisfy `isRoutineComment` in `compactTimelineEvents` (app/server/tasks/timeline-compaction.server.ts:89-97: non-human actor, `toAgent: false`, not a marker), so on a long task they fold into "N earlier routine comments compacted". The typed `transition` event is written only when a move is *executed*; the typed resolution event only when a packet is *answered*.
gaps.why_it_matters: The outcome of a decision always survives, so this is the mildest of the five — but on a long-running task the record can end up showing that a stage move happened without showing that it was proposed, or showing a resolved decision without the request that framed it. The PRD names "transition requests" as one of the five typed important-event classes precisely so this class of record is never compacted away.
gaps.intent_basis: MVP Phase-1 bullet "Typed important events for quality flags, transition requests, blocked decisions, completion reports, and policy violations"; FR16; FR33 (reconstruct "who initiated a consequential action"); the compaction contract in timeline-compaction.server.ts:10-11 ("preserving EVERY typed governance event").
gaps.evidence_of_absence: All `type: "transition"` producers are stage moves, packet resolutions and packet withdrawals (grep across app/server, 12 sites); none fires on `addRecommendation`. `compactTimelineEvents` explicitly preserves human comments and every typed event and folds everything else machine-authored.
gaps.owner_question: Should an operator recommendation and an `input`-type packet write typed events (e.g. `transition` for a recommended move, `blocked`/a new type for a decision request) so they are exempt from compaction, or is the executed outcome a sufficient permanent record?
gaps.partial:
PARTIALLY EXISTS. What is there:

1. A PRECEDENT ALREADY SHIPS. F19-1's `recordDeliveredNextStep` (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:3966-3979) creates the SAME `kind: "transition"` recommendation card after a successful delivery and narrates it as `type: "note"` with `actor {kind: "system", systemId: "delivery"}` — a typed, compaction-immune event. So one transition-request producer is already typed; the operator's own path simply does not follow it. This is the shape of the fix, not a new invention.

2. THE PENDING REQUEST IS NEVER LOST. While pending, the request lives in `frontmatter.recommendations[]` / `frontmatter.packet` — structured task-file state compaction does not touch, and the card, bell, "Waiting on you" inbox and board chip all read from it. What compaction erases is only the HISTORICAL narration; the live decision surface is safe. The claim overstates if read as "a pending request can disappear".

3. AUDIT ROWS EXIST BUT ARE INVISIBLE. `task.operator.recommended` (operator-actions.server.ts:485, 584), `task.operator.recommended_completion` (:2587), `task.operator.packet_opened` (:837), `task.recommendation.applied` (task-actions.server.ts:5921) and `task.recommendation.dismissed` are all recorded and never compacted. But NONE of them appears in `AUDIT_ACTION_KINDS` (app/server/projections/activity-feed.server.ts:113-150), so none renders anywhere in the UI — reconstructing "who requested this move" needs raw SQLite. FR33 also bounds audit to 90 days while asserting task-scoped history "is also written to the canonical `task.md` and survives indefinitely" — which is exactly the copy compaction removes.

4. THE LOSS PROPAGATES TO THE ACTIVITY STREAM. `listActivityStream` reads `task_events`, which is DELETEd and reinserted from `task.md` on every reproject (app/server/projections/rebuilder.server.ts:505-508), so a folded request also disappears from the cross-task Activity stream, not just the task timeline.

5. THE UI LABEL ALREADY EXISTS FOR THE MISSING SEMANTIC. `app/features/task-detail/event-meta.ts:34` renders the typed `transition` event with the pill label "Transition request" — but that type only ever fires on an executed move or a packet withdrawal. And the `compression-threshold` guardrail's own settings copy promises "typed events are always kept" (app/shared/workflow/templates.ts:86): true, but the request narration is not typed, so the promise does not cover it.

6. ADJACENT AND ARGUABLY WORSE: `dismissRecommendation` (app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:~5967-5985) writes NO timeline event at all — only an audit row. A dismissed transition request therefore leaves zero trace in the canonical file regardless of compaction, so "the operator proposed moving to Review and a human declined" is unreconstructable from `task.md` even on a short task.

Net: the typed-event vocabulary, the compaction contract and a working system-authored precedent all exist; the gap is narrowly that the OPERATOR's own request writers (`addRecommendation`, and the `input` branch of `operatorOpenPacket`) emit `type: "comment"` instead of a typed event, plus the dismissal path emitting nothing at all.

gaps.title: A continuity failure reaches no human — one timeline row is the entire signal

The only remedy is for a human to clone and rebase outside Viberr, which contradicts the single-writer invariant (the delivering engagement is sole owner of the workspace, branch and PR), is invisible to the app until the next reconcile, and is exactly the "reconstruct the truth outside the product" failure the UX spec names as make-or-break.

gaps.title: Nothing detects or displays a task that has quietly stopped moving
gaps.what_is_absent: No surface shows how long a task has been in its current state, and nothing in the system notices a task that stopped progressing. There is no last-activity display on any board card, review row or task page, and no idle/stall detector of any kind.
gaps.why_it_matters: The board is specified as a triage-first Signal Console whose job is to say what needs a human. A task whose operator turn ended without queuing anything, whose run errored after the file was written, or that is simply waiting on an agent nobody re-engaged, renders identically to one being actively worked — right down to a pulsing 'agent working' dot. Supervising several live tasks (Journey 1) means the failure mode is silent: the tasks that need attention are precisely the ones that stopped producing events, and they are the least visible things on the board. Past passes fixed individual stranding causes (pass 11's transition re-trigger, R18-2's post-delivery re-queue) one at a time; there is still no backstop that notices the general case.
gaps.intent_basis: FR24 (cards show waiting state, human vs agent); UX principles 'Status before history' and 'Human attention is scarce — only interrupt when judgment is required'; PRD Journey 1 (supervise several persistent agent threads without losing the thread); NFR reliability intent that runtime failures degrade visibly rather than silently.
gaps.evidence_of_absence: `TaskSummary.updatedAt` is projected (`app/shared/mapping/task.server.ts:142`) and consumed by nothing: grepping `updatedAt` across `app/features` and `app/routes` returns only the Home project card (`app/features/home/project-cards.tsx:98-102`, a project-level label) and org-settings resource rows. The board card's `WaitTag` (`app/features/board/board-page.tsx:128-148`) renders "agent working" with an animated `.working` dot purely from the stored `task.waiting` field — it never consults the live run registry, even though that registry is already queried elsewhere (`app/features/home/home-query.server.ts:189-196` counts `agent_runs WHERE state='running'` per project, and `operatorSnapshot.liveRuns` hands it to the operator). Grepping `stalled|idle|no activity|watchdog` across the board feature and projections returns nothing. The one background nudge that exists (`app/server/github/reconcile-poller.server.ts:30-92`) covers a single terminal case — an accepted task whose PR is still open — which proves the poller-plus-notification machinery is in place and applied to exactly one situation.

gaps.title: What a run was actually given is not inspectable in the app

gaps.why_it_matters: Murat's whole job in Journey 4 is to confirm the canonical file holds enough context to continue safely — but the thing the agent actually receives is a truncated projection of that file he cannot see. The same blind spot sits under a class of problem the passes keep rediscovering: a KB grant that resolves to nothing (pass 13's silent-resource class), the Claude-vs-Codex skills asymmetry the product promises to disclose rather than hide (R18-5), and the KB-vs-repo precedence rule (R19-2). Every one of those is a claim about what an agent was given, and the only way to check any of them today is to export the session and resume it locally — which FR23 explicitly frames as a debug escape hatch, not the primary record.
gaps.intent_basis: FR22 / NFR12 (a reactivated agent continues from canonical task state; graceful degradation when runtime history is gone); FR23 (the provider-native session is for deep debugging, not the primary record); PRD Journey 4; R18-5 and R19-2, both of which are disclosure promises about run inputs.
gaps.evidence_of_absence: `canonicalTaskAnchor` (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts:957+`) is the re-anchor mechanism — a clamped goal, the open packet, and the newest N timeline entries each truncated by `anchorClamp` — and nothing renders it. gaps.title: A human cannot correct or withdraw a claim recorded in the canonical record
gaps.what_is_absent: The task record is append-only for humans in the app. There is no way to edit, delete, retract, or mark-as-incorrect a timeline entry — including an agent's factual claim about work it did — and no event type or field that expresses 'this was superseded / this is wrong'.
gaps.why_it_matters: The record is not just a display: `canonicalTaskAnchor` feeds recent timeline text back into every agent resume, and the operator snapshot re-reads comments each turn. A wrong agent claim ('the suite passes', 'the endpoint returns X') therefore keeps being re-injected as canonical context for the rest of the task's life. A human's only recourse is to append a contradicting comment and hope the model weighs recency correctly — which is exactly the memory-drift risk the PRD names. The file-level escape hatch (FR10: edit task.md on disk, the watcher reprojects) exists, but it needs shell access to the data root, writes no audit row, and is unavailable to a teammate using the web app.
gaps.intent_basis: UX principle 'One task, one truth — the canonical record is the trusted coordination surface'; FR12 (canonical record) and FR17 (compressed history preserving continuity); FR33 (auditable history of human decisions and agent actions); the PRD's named risk that persistent agent memory becomes stale or unsafe.
gaps.evidence_of_absence: The task route's action intents (`app/routes/project.task.tsx:319-799`) are comment, update-goal, resolve-packet, complete-merge, accept-completion, deliver-review, archive/restore-task, force-accept, owner-take/assign/release, transition, run-interrupt, assign/run specialist and reviewer, remove-reviewer, apply/dismiss-recommendation, run-operator, schedule-action, cancel-schedule — nothing that touches an existing timeline entry. `TIMELINE_EVENT_TYPES` (`app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts:47-66`) has no correction or retraction type, and `TaskFileEvent` carries no superseded/disputed field. Compaction (`app/server/tasks/timeline-compaction.server.ts`) can fold an agent reply into a count-only marker but never offers a correction path. The goal, notably, *is* correctable (`update-goal`) — the gap is specific to recorded events.
gaps.owner_question: Should a human be able to strike a recorded agent claim — as an audited correction event that supersedes the original in the anchor while leaving both visible — or is append-only the deliberate contract, with the on-disk edit as the sole escape hatch?
gaps.partial:
PARTIAL — precisely what is there and what is not.

EXISTS (correction/withdrawal machinery, all acting on LIVE STATE, never on a recorded event):
- Goal: `update-goal` (task-actions.server.ts:541-609) rewrites the canonical goal in place, appends a `note` event "Goal updated", audits task.goal.updated, re-engages the operator with a `goal-updated` trigger. The goal is the one correctable part of the record, as claimed.
- Packets: `resolve_decision_packet` lets the operator WITHDRAW its own moot packet with a reason written to the timeline (toolkit :344-345); `withdrawSupersededStuckPacket` (task-actions.server.ts:1718-1790, audit `task.packet.withdrawn_superseded`, test agent-completion.server.test.ts:775) does it server-side. It refuses to withdraw an agent-raised question.
- Recommendations: `dismiss-recommendation` (audit task.recommendation.dismissed) discards an agent proposal.
- Schedules: `cancel-schedule` sets status `cancelled` and RETAINS the row (SCHEDULE_STATUS_VALUES; verified live in NOTES.md UC-18) — the nearest existing model of "withdrawn but still visible", but it governs a pending action, not a statement.
- Contradiction flagging exists only between a knowledge base and the repo: `flag_context_conflict` (toolkit :217-250) records "these two sources disagree, here is which won". There is no analogue for "this timeline claim disagrees with reality".
- Compaction (timeline-compaction.server.ts) folds agent replies into count-only markers — it shrinks history, never marks anything false.
- Append-a-correction: a human can post a follow-up `comment`; force-accept and rejection paths append their own typed events. The record can be argued with, never annotated.

DOES NOT EXIST:
- No intent, tool, action or audit verb that edits, deletes, retracts, redacts or annotates an already-recorded timeline event — including an agent's factual claim about work it did.
- No event type and no field expressing "superseded" / "disputed" / "corrected by". A reader six weeks later sees a false agent completion report rendered identically to a true one; the only signal is a later comment they must find and correlate themselves.
- Nothing binds a correction to what it corrects. Even where the product already knows a claim was doubted — pass 19's N19-7 (NOTES.md:103-110), where the reviewer explicitly refused to treat a delivering agent's self-report as proof — that refusal lands as an unlinked separate event.

ONE ESCAPE HATCH WORTH NAMING: task.md is watched (file-watch.service.server.ts:84 explicitly admits `task.md` through the ignore filter) and the parser is tolerant, so anyone with filesystem access to VIBERR_DATA_ROOT can edit or delete a timeline entry by hand and the app reprojects it silently — no audit row, no actor, no trace that the record changed. That is the inverse of a governed correction path: the record is append-only to everyone who follows the rules and freely rewritable by anyone who does not.

NOT PREVIOUSLY DECIDED: I found no ruling in docs/architecture/decisions.md (58 rulings) and no entry in INTENT.md's divergence list declaring the timeline deliberately immutable. This looks like an unexamined default rather than a decision, so it is a genuine gap, not a re-litigation.

gaps.title: No non-destructive upgrade path: the migration ledger is filename-only and the schema is a re-squashed baseline
gaps.what_is_absent: There is no mechanism that lets an existing deployment take a new app version's schema. Missing: a checksum/content hash in the migration ledger, any second migration file, a boot-time guard that detects the baseline changed under an already-migrated DB, and any mention of the hazard in the operator-facing upgrade procedure. The ruling's own instruction to "revisit this convention at the first real deployment" has not been executed, and there is no cut-over that starts a forward-only chain.
gaps.why_it_matters: This is the first operational event a self-hosting team hits after go-live: a new version ships. Today the upgrade either silently runs an old schema against new code (SQL errors on writes touching new columns, with no boot warning) or requires the documented wipe — and deployment.md itself explains that wiping projection.sqlite re-mints user ids while `members[].userId` / `ownerUserId` in the canonical task files keep the old ones, so "every membership and task owner becomes a ghost" with "no re-mapping tool". Every PAT, session, and the whole audit trail go with it. The product ships a Dockerfile, compose.yml and a deployment guide that invite self-hosting, so the pre-prod convention is now load-bearing in a way it was not designed to be.
gaps.intent_basis: docs/operations/deployment.md §Upgrades promises upgrades and rollbacks against the same volume; planning/planning-artifacts/architecture.md:661 and :780 record the squash convention as valid only "while pre-production" and "forward-only after first deploy"; INTENT.md divergence 20 makes projection.sqlite primary storage, not a cache.

Migrations apply at boot" — the wipe-and-reseat requirement appears nowhere in docs/operations/.

WHAT EXISTS (the claim's "no mechanism that lets an existing deployment take a new app version's schema" is too strong):

1. The runner already supports a forward-only chain. `runMigrations` reads every `*.sql` in the directory, sorts by filename, skips recorded ones, and applies the rest each in its own transaction (`app/server/db/migration-runner.server.ts:39-78`). Dropping a `0002_*.sql` into `db/migrations/` tomorrow would apply cleanly to an already-migrated DB with no code change. This is not theory — `app/server/db/migration-runner.server.test.ts` has a test "applies migrations in filename order" that writes `0001_first.sql` + `0002_second.sql` into a temp dir and asserts both apply in order, and a test "is idempotent" asserting the second run applies nothing. So the cut-over the claim says is missing requires adding a file, not building machinery.

2. Migration failure is safe and typed: the whole file plus its bookkeeping row roll back together, and a typed `AppError` with `ERROR_CODES.DB_MIGRATION_FAILED` (`app/server/errors/error-codes.ts:12`) is thrown with `details: { migration }`. A test asserts the failed migration leaves zero rows in `schema_migrations` so a fixed file re-applies.

3. Boot emits migration state: `logBootIntegrity` (`app/server/boot.server.ts:49-71`) logs `migrationsApplied` (count) and `latestMigration` (max filename), and `docs/operations/runbook.md:19-20` tells the operator to grep that line after a deploy. But it is an observability line, not a guard — it reports the recorded *filename*, which by construction cannot change when the baseline's *content* changes.

4. The squash convention itself is deliberate and documented as time-boxed: `planning/planning-artifacts/architecture.md:780-782` ("deliberate and time-boxed: after the first real deployment, migrations become additive and forward-only") and the header of `db/migrations/0001_baseline.sql:10-20`, which spells out the exact hazard and the recovery ("wipe the sqlite and re-seed (`npm run seed -- --reset`)") and ends "Revisit this convention at the first real deployment."
